archetype.name: Title Contender (frontcourt-driven)
archetype.definition: A team whose results already look like a top-three side, built on an elite big-man group and offensive rebounding rather than volume three-point shooting, with the record fully backed by its margin.

report.headline: The offense leads the league, though the jumpers are running hot
report.take:
Houston has opened 6-1 with the second-best Net Rtg in the league at 12.6, and nothing about it is a close-game mirage. The W vs Pt Diff sits at 0 and the margin implies 6 wins, exactly what they have. The one loss came by five at Dallas. The wins include an 18-point home win over Dallas, a 32-point rout in Milwaukee and a 21-point win over Oklahoma City. That last result matters most: it says this isn't just a soft opening schedule. This is a team that went 52-30 in each of the last two seasons and has stepped up again, now third on the site's Teams tab.

The change is on offense. Houston was 13th and then 8th in Off Rank the last two years and is first now, with an ORtg of 122.6 against a league mean of 113. Part of that is the familiar identity. The Rockets still take few threes (3PA Rate 38.1, 26th) and still crash the offensive glass (ORB % 32.4, third, right in line with last year's 34.8). They are also getting to the line more than in recent years (FT Rate 31.8, eighth). The engine is the frontcourt, graded A+. Alperen Şengün is second on the center tab with a 6.1 BPM and a +22.3 On-Off. Jabari Smith Jr. is fourth at power forward, with 21 threes on 64.6 TS %. Kevin Durant leads the team with 154 points on 65.5 TS %.

The numbers flatter them in two places. The first is shooting: a 39 3P % (third) against last season's 36.4, plus guard lines like Marcus Smart's 75.6 TS % and Bogdan Bogdanović's 70.1, are not levels a low-volume three-point team usually holds. The second is defense, which is quietly worse than its 10th-ranked DRtg suggests. Opponents are shooting just 30.2% from three, fourth-lowest, while hitting 69.7% at the rim, 24th and well above Houston's 64.5 last year. The rim defense is the real issue. The three-point luck is the cushion hiding it.

Where it heads: the shooting will cool, and the 70-win pace is a seven-game artifact. The foundation is sturdy, though. A frontcourt this deep, a repeatable rebounding edge and a defense that has finished top 10 for three straight years point to a team that settles in as one of the West's best rather than one that fades.

strengths.title: Elite, deep frontcourt carrying everything
strengths.body: Three of the league's top six power forwards and centers by the site's rankings play here, and the group is the only A+ on the roster. Şengün runs the offense from the post with team-best playmaking, while Smith and Durant both score efficiently around him. Because the talent is spread across several players rather than one, this should hold even when individual shooting cools.

strengths.title: Second chances as a system
strengths.body: Houston rebounds its own misses at the third-best rate in the league. That isn't new: it was 34.8% last season and 31.7% the year before. It reflects size and intent, so it is the most bankable part of the offense. It also gives the Rockets possessions back when the jumpers stop falling.

strengths.title: Margin fully earns the record
strengths.body: The record isn't built on coin-flip finishes. The W vs Pt Diff is 0, and the scoring margin per game ranks second. Even the last five games, which included the loss, held the margin at 13 a game, so there's no fragile luck to unwind.

concerns.title: Rim defense has slipped badly
concerns.body: Opponents are converting 69.7% within four feet, 24th in the league and far worse than Houston allowed last year. The defense ranks 10th mainly because opponents have shot only 30.2% from three. That figure tends to drift back toward the league's 34.9 over time. If it drifts and the rim numbers don't improve, the DRtg will climb.

concerns.title: Unsustainable perimeter shooting
concerns.body: A 39 3P % from a team that takes threes less often than almost anyone is well above Houston's recent history. It is also propped up by small-sample hot hands in the guard rotation. Expect the shooting to come back down and the league-best offense to settle closer to its very good level of last season.

concerns.title: Guards and wings score freely
concerns.body: Opposing shooting guards and small forwards account for far more of the points against Houston than the league norm. Power forwards barely score at all. Some of that is how opponents attack a big front line, but the SF points allowed rank 28th. A thin wing group, with Amen Thompson posting a -37 On-Off in a tiny sample, is the soft spot.

trend.note: The Rockets have been dominant from opening night, winning five straight before the Dallas loss and then routing OKC. The last five games ran right at the season's margin, with no fade or surge.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, but Boston and Minnesota test them
weekAhead.body:
Houston plays three of four at home, but the first two opponents are real: Boston ranks fifth in Net Rtg and Minnesota fourth. Minnesota is far better than its 4-3 suggests, carrying the league's worst W vs Pt Diff and the fourth-best DRtg. Those two games will say more about this team than the season so far has.

The back half is kinder. Phoenix has the league's worst defense and worst defensive rebounding. Denver ranks 21st in DRtg and lets opponents get to the rim more than almost anyone. A 3-1 week is the reasonable expectation, and the glass is Houston's edge in all four games.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's glass vs Boston's weakness
keyMatchups.body: Boston ranks 27th in DRB %, and Houston is third in ORB %. That is the cleanest mismatch on the schedule. Boston's F-graded wings also give up the most threes in the league to small forwards, an opening for Thompson.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's defense, unlucky record
keyMatchups.body: The Wolves allow 105.9 points per 100 possessions, fourth-best, and they shut down opposing small forwards and power forwards. Their weak spot is centers, where scoring allowed ranks 20th. That points the offense toward Şengün. This is the week's hardest game.

keyMatchups.title: Phoenix's frontcourt can't hold up
keyMatchups.body: Phoenix has the worst DRtg in the league and an F frontcourt. It concedes more rebounds to centers than anyone, which sets up a big night for Şengün and Capela if Capela's day-to-day status clears. Only a cold shooting night keeps this game close.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Houston's rim defense tightens against Minnesota and Denver, two teams that can punish it inside.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the offense to come back from first in the league toward the top-five range. The three-point percentage and some guard efficiency lines will regress, but the offensive rebounding, rising free-throw rate and frontcourt depth are real and travel. The defense is the bigger swing. Its 10th-place rank is propped up by opponent three-point misses, while its rim protection is the worst of the Udoka era seasons on this sheet. If that improves toward last year's level, Houston is a genuine top-two seed. If not, the margin shrinks toward last season's.

On balance this looks like a team modestly better than the 52-win versions of the last two years. A final win total in the mid-50s, with a Net Rtg settling in the 6.5 to 9 range, fits what is real here while discounting a seven-game shooting spike.
swingFactors: Rim protection returning to last season's level
How far the three-point shooting cools

confidence.note: Only seven games, but the margin matches the record and the style matches recent seasons.
